headline: Recommended $43,500,000 in bonds for a public works garage, plus $5,000,000 for pools and $4,275,000 for sewer work.
summary: Alderman Johnson opposed most items, and debate focused on the garage's cost and on interest paid on bonds. The items now go to the full Board of Aldermen, and the chairman said the garage bonds will need ten votes there.
decisions: Recommended final passage of bonds up to $43,500,000 for a Public Works garage and fleet maintenance facility; Johnson opposed and Kelly abstained.
Recommended moving up to $3,183,200 in unused bond money to the Public Works garage project; Johnson and Thibeault opposed and Kelly abstained.
Recommended final passage of up to $3,000,000 in bonds or a state loan for wastewater treatment plant Phase 1 upgrades; Johnson opposed.
Recommended final passage of up to $4,275,000 in bonds for sewer infrastructure and drain casting replacement; Johnson opposed.
Recommended final passage of up to $2,550,000 in bonds for various wastewater capital improvements; Johnson opposed.
Recommended final passage of up to $2,000,000 in bonds for improvements at the Four Hills Landfill; Johnson opposed.
Recommended final passage of up to $2,678,828 in bonds to buy solid waste capital equipment; Johnson opposed.
Recommended final passage of up to $5,000,000 in bonds to repair and renovate two public inground swimming pools; Johnson opposed.

BUDGET REVIEW COMMITTEE 
 
OCTOBER 6, 2026 
 
A meeting of the Budget Review Committee was held Tuesday, October 6, 2026 at 8:55 p.m. in the Aldermanic Chamber 
and duly noticed in two places, including the City’s website, in accordance with the requirements of R SA 91-A:2 II. 
 
Alderman Richard A. Dowd, Chairman, presided.

ON THE QUESTION 
 
Alderman Thibeault  
 
Thank you, Mr. Chair.  One thing I wanted to correct that was in Public Comment earlier is that someone said that every 
single one of the bonds tonight would pass no problem because most of the Board endorsed it.  Six - mo st of these things 
are six or seven Aldermen endorsing it.  So that's just not true.  That leaves eight or nine left to endorse - I mean to say 
yes.  So you never know.  People change their minds  so I just don't want people to think that all these are just rubber 
stamps.  We think about them.  
 
For this particular one, the ultimate cost of this going to $53 million - that's a lot of money.  Imagine what we could do for 
the homeless with just a few of those millions, right, but we don't have that project on here, right, or - I know we have the 
resource center coming maybe.  But it's a lot of mo ney here.  We passed up a resource center for just a few million 
dollars.  So this is a lot of money.  People are going to say, "Oh, you can you can store vehicles.  You can keep them 
nice and warm and toasty with radiant heating but what about the people that are out in the cold."  So I mean that's all 
great.  I mean half these numbers that I'm looking at, I mean, they're guesses to a certain extent.  T hey're all guesses.  I 
mean we say it when we're any of these projects that when we ask the question, well where are you gett ing that number 
and they're like well, you know, we're looking at this year and we're adding some inflation to it, and you know, I guess 
that's where it's going to be, and by the way if you do this in 10 years, it's going to be $300 million to do.  Okay.  Well I get 
that.  Of course everything goes up, right?  So I get that.  Every time you pass off something a year, it's going to go up.  I 
understand that but some of these numbers - you don't have finite numbers because we haven't got the b id out yet and 
people haven't bid on it.  
 
So usually we try to go above and beyond because we  want to make sure we don't go over and we want to make sure we 
have some surplus.  I get that as well.  So I just think it's a lot of money and I think people are going to question it out 
there.  I believe it's in the bonding plan as far as we're not going to go out and just sell $53 million dollars of bonds 
tomorrow.  It's going to be planned over the time of hopefully to make it $25 million per year because that's what's in our 
average $25 million per year.  But I mean that's where I'm coming at it from.  I'm not saying I'm not voting for it but 
because I originally endorsed it as well but when I come to start thinking about the money we're spending on this, it's a lot 
for this and we don't - we can guess on how much it saves in keeping a car out of the cold but how muc h does it really 
save?  I know people will come up with things.  I read this in this magazine or that in this magazine, yada yada, whatever, 
but it's hard to quantify that in actual dollars, I think.   So we'll see if I actually endorse or vote on it or not.  We'll see. 
 
Chairman Dowd 
 
Two things.  One - the final vote will be at the Board of Aldermen.  It will need ten votes. 
 
And the other is that we did have a presentation as we were going along about from qualified sources a bout the 
maintenance of equipment, and cold starts versus stored vehicles inside, and the money we save in in saving vehicles, 
and keeping them longer, and maintenance is probabl y going to pay most of the debt service, so.   
 
Alderman Thibeault  
 
I've seen them all and I know but we're still voting it for tonight not just at the Board of Aldermen.  
 
Chairman Dowd

expanding our facilities group in the budget.  We j ust approved a Facilities Manager that we'll be hiring in January and

stewards of our capital assets as much as possible.  So making sure we have that operational plan is fundamental.  I 
submit to you that that that commitment is not going to waver because we recognize how truly important  it is and we are 
working within the constrained resources that we have to prioritize it, but it's it is a big priority for us.

moment and reassure this body that the numbers that  you're seeing before you for the hard construction costs have been

the numbers before you now have been studied dilige ntly over the last few weeks.  If you'd like, I could have the Owner's

at that $43 million figure if you'd like.

Chairman Dowd 
 
Alderman Gregg.

Thank you.  So I think that obviously this is this amount of money is always hard to swallow but I do t hink that when we 
are being diligent with our duties here and how we invest the tax dollars which we're all taxpayers too, it's what does that 
return look like?  I do think that this project is a strategic project for the City because it looks f orward.  It's not just trying to 
fill in a gap or whatever.

building is literally crumbling.  Something has to happen.  So rather than just build something that will be another 
temporary fix, which that was supposed to be, this invests in the future of our City.
Budget Review Committee – 10/06/2026   Page 5 
 
As far as whether or not you know we're taking into account money for the homeless or any other project  in the City, this 
is also a very big important project because there isn't anything in this City that touches anyone.  The DPW doesn't have 
a hand in every single day and we're talking about efficiencies in getting our first responders when we have snow days, 
having that all at one facility, which we've talked about.  We could rehash all of this but I think that yes, this is a big cost 
but this is a cost that's going to save in a lot of ways.  It's also looking forward as the City builds, as we continue to grow.  
As we do have more housing, we're going to need the se services much more organized and this looks forw ard to that.  I 
think DPW has done an amazing job at lining out this project, figuring out where they could cut, where they could not cut, 
and how to make this the best that it can be for the City.  So I do think it's a lot of money but it's the type of investment 
that we should be looking at for the City. 
 
Chairman Dowd 
 
Alderman Thibeault.  
 
Alderman Thibeault  
 
Thank you, Mr. Chair.  I think we've all toured the facility.  We know it's terrible.  I don't think that's in doubt at all but like I 
said, people dying out on the streets is just as important as putting trucks in a garage.  I've been for this the whole time so 
I don't want to - I'm not necessarily changing my view on it but I don't want to minimize that either.  We turned down a 
resource center.  People literally in this horseshoe right now turned down for a few million dollars, so including myself.  
So I get it.  We need this.  We absolutely need this.  
 
And my other point is really about the maintenance.  Well, just two things.  So the maintenance and the savings.  I think 
the hard cost may be a real number but the savings isn't.  Like we don't really know.  I mean it was a $25 million to $40 
million.  That's a big gap in savings over 50 years.  So that's a big gap.  You know, 40 would be great.  It’s still not even a 
million a year.  So that's concerning because you're never going to know exactly until the saving starts coming in on that.   
 
Maintenance-wise, that's great that we're putting forward thinking on maintaining our buildings and infrastructures in the 
City.  What about when you get a new Mayor in here?  What about when you get new Aldermen and new heads  of 
things?  That doesn't mean they're not going to pay attention to maintenance.  So just because we're t hinking about it 
doesn't mean the next administration or administrations down the road are going to have the same feelings as us about 
maintenance.  So how do we guarantee that things wi ll be maintained or this building will be maintained?  We don't have 
that.  Obviously, this one wasn't.  So someone left it to just rot because it is in bad shape.  So I think if I say yes to this 
tonight, it's going to be with a caveat that I'm st ill going to be thinking about this leading up to the Board of Aldermen 
meeting to decide whether I'm going to be one of those 10 votes when we get there.  Our track record o f having all 15 
here isn't always good.  So I don't know if that still means we have to have 10 or if it's a percentage of the whole.  I'm not 
even sure about that but yeah, so if I vote yes tonight, it doesn't mean I'm voting yes at the Board of Aldermen. 
 
Chairman Dowd 
 
So relative to maintenance - when that building was built, the materials weren't built for maintaining.  The two high 
schools were built 20 years ago, and people go in them today and they look brand new because they were built to be 
maintained, and they are maintained as well as all of our new schools.  So - and as we heard from the c ontractor and 
from sustainability, they're putting a lot of effort into making sure this building is not only maintainable but has a huge 
savings relative to health benefits, emissions, you know, things that we've been on this Board asking for a long, long time 
when we build a building.  Alderman from Ward 5 use d to always be after these sustainability things well this building will 
support - we heard from people on the sustainability issue.  It's built the last.  It's built to last and they said 50 years.  The 
high school and that we've been and middle school at Elm Street lasted almost 100 years and that was b uilt under war 
funds.  So things have changed.  The building materia ls today are built to be maintained easily, and last, and I think the 
savings are – if you just take the savings in Public Health from the employees that are working there, that's critically 
important to me.  These people deserve a good place to work.  Yes, it's nice we're going to keep the equipment longer 
and that saves us money.  So there's a lot of ways with savings.  
 
Now can you quantify it to the dollar?  Hell no.  W e don't know what's going on with the economy especially now.  And as 
far as other Boards are concerned, those two high schools have been through multiple Boards of Alderme n and they're 
maintained.  So I don't think that's an issue.  Any other comments? 
 
MOTION CARRIED (Alderman Johnson in opposition, Alderwoman Kelly a bstained)
